title: The Delayed Stabilizer ZX-Calculus
abstract: Many stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes are built from a finite pattern repeated across space or time, such as lattice codes, translation-invariant graph states, and quantum convolutional codes. Ordinary stabilizer ZX-diagrams capture only finite truncations of such systems, obscuring the repeated structure that defines them. We introduce the delayed stabilizer ZX-calculus, a finite graphical language for these infinite, translation-invariant processes. It extends the odd-prime-dimensional stabilizer ZX-calculus with a single new generator, the delay, which feeds data from one time step to the next. We equip the calculus with two semantics. In the first semantics, we interpret the behaviour of a delayed ZX-diagram as an equivalence class of sequences of quantum channels; where two sequences are identified if they have the same information content. We show that the behaviour of a delayed ZX-diagram uniquely determines an infinite stabilizer group. In the second semantics, we interpret the delay as a formal variable, encoding the translation-invariant families of Pauli operators as generating functions. This allows us to represent a delayed ZX-diagram in terms of a tableau of generating functions, from which the infinite stabilizer group can be recovered. Finally, we give a complete axiomatization of the delayed stabilizer ZX-calculus, featuring generalised Euler decomposition and colour change rules. Using generalised forms of local complementation and pivoting, we reduce every diagram to a unique normal form. This establishes soundness, universality, and completeness for the generating tableau semantics.
summary: The paper develops the delayed stabilizer ZX-calculus ($\delta$ZX) to overcome the limitations of standard diagrams when modeling infinitely repeating quantum structures like lattice codes. By introducing a 'delay' generator and defining two formal semantics, it provides a complete algebraic framework for representing and simplifying these infinite processes into unique canonical forms.
main_problem: Ordinary stabilizer ZX-diagrams are insufficient for modeling quantum processes that exhibit infinite, translation-invariant structures across space or time.
main_result: The authors introduce the delayed stabilizer ZX-calculus ($\delta$ZX), establishing a unique normal form and proving soundness, universality, and completeness for its generating tableau semantics.
method: The calculus extends the standard ZX-diagram formalism with a 'delay' generator ($\delta$), allowing the representation of infinite processes via formal variables encoding generating functions.
model_or_system: The theory models stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes and general translation-invariant quantum circuits, originally formulated for qudits based on an odd prime $p$. The formalism relates these physical systems to algebraic structures like affine Lagrangian subspaces.
key_observables: Infinite stabilizer groups; equivalence classes of sequences of quantum channels; generating functions encoding Pauli operators.
important_parameters: The delay parameter ($\delta$); the dimension related to an odd prime $p$; matrix entries in the field $\mathbb{F}_p(\delta)$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that infinite, translation-invariant processes can be captured by extending the finite ZX calculus with a formal delay variable.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate axioms of the standard ZX calculus encoding Pauli operators ($Z^z X^x$) and provide examples for various quantum states (e.g., Bell states).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the foundational equivalence between stabilizer mechanics, symplectic linear algebra, and the standard ZX-calculus. It then develops the delayed calculus by introducing $\delta$, providing two semantics (channel sequences and generating functions), and finally proving a complete reduction to a unique normal form via matrix algebra techniques.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful mathematical tool for analyzing large-scale quantum systems, such as those found in solid-state or photonic implementations of QEC codes, by providing a rigorous way to handle infinite periodic boundary conditions.
